title: AI Benchmarks: How Models Are Tested

scenes.text: Every new AI model launches with a chart, showing it beat everyone else. [1] But what are those tests, and can you trust them? [2] Let's understand AI benchmarks.
A benchmark is a standard exam for AI models. [1] It's a fixed set of questions with known answers, [2] every model takes the same test, [3] and the scores let us compare them fairly.

data.definition: A standard set of test questions with known answers, used to compare AI models fairly.

scenes.text: Here are some popular ones. [1] MMLU tests general knowledge, across dozens of school and college subjects. [2] Math benchmarks test step by step problem solving. [3] Coding benchmarks check whether the model's code actually passes tests. [4] And chatbot arenas let real people vote on which answer they prefer.

There are two styles of testing. [1] Automatic tests have exact answers, so they're fast and cheap. [2] Human preference tests, like arenas, capture what people actually like, but they're slower, and can reward confident sounding answers.

But benchmarks have problems. [1] Contamination, when test questions leak into the training data, so the model has seen the answers. [2] Saturation, when every top model scores near 100 percent, so the test stops being useful. [3] And gaming, when models are tuned just to score high, not to be useful.
So how should you judge a model? [1] Look at several benchmarks, not just one. [2] Check community reviews, and arena rankings. [3] And most importantly, test it on your own real tasks.

Here's a common myth. [1] People think the model with the highest benchmark score is the best for everything. [2] A model can top one chart, and still be worse at your task. Benchmarks are a starting point, not a final answer.

data.myth: The highest benchmark score means the best model for everything.
data.fact: A model can top one chart and still be worse at your task. Benchmarks are a starting point.
